[TIMING CAVEAT: published 17:00 BST Friday, i.e. ONE HOUR BEFORE the 18:00 cut-off. Sky News re-ran it as a fresh video package overnight/this morning. Treat as carry-over unless the evening brief omitted it.]

HEADLINE: Discovery of 97 million files related to SAS inquiry 'regrettable', MoD says

FACTS:
- The discovery of 97 million documents more than three years into an inquiry investigating allegations that UK special forces committed war crimes in Afghanistan was a "regrettable failure", the Ministry of Defence has said.
- The inquiry's chair, Lord Justice Haddon-Cave, called the discovery "troubling" and "extraordinary news".
- The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan (IIA) was established in 2022 to investigate alleged executions by members of the Special Air Service between 2010 and 2013, during so-called night raids targeting the Taliban. It has yet to produce any findings.
- MoD lawyers were called to a hearing ON FRIDAY 25 SEPTEMBER to explain why the documents from the period in question were not found sooner.
- Haddon-Cave said he had taken the "exceptional step" of calling the hearing because of the disclosure and the "somewhat casual way" the MoD had informed his team.
- Within the new files, the MoD says it has identified thousands of potentially relevant documents, including images that appear to have been taken during a number of special forces operations under investigation. It stressed much of the material would be unrelated to the inquiry's terms of reference.
- The IIA told the BBC it was yet to receive any of the new material.
- Haddon-Cave said he intended to call another hearing NEXT MONTH to question the MoD on its progress, and that he had set a deadline to hear all evidence by 30 APRIL 2027, seeking assurances the new discovery would not delay the inquiry further.
- The inquiry was set up by the then-Defence Secretary Ben Wallace following BBC Panorama reporting in 2022. It had stated it would provide an interim or final report 12-18 months after being established; after almost four years it has yet to publish any findings.
- The BBC revealed earlier this month the inquiry has already cost the public purse £58m. Around half is understood to be money spent by the MoD and wider government responding to the inquiry, including lawyers representing former SAS officers and senior military figures.
- Comparison: the Grenfell Tower inquiry took more than seven years and cost more than £170m.
- SAS night-time arrest raids in Afghanistan were called Deliberate Detention Operations (DDOs). After a raid, SAS members and support staff took photos of anyone killed and collected mobile phones and other devices. Forensic experts are examining these images to see whether the SAS's account fits the ballistic evidence visible in the photographs.

QUOTE (Steven Gray KC, representing the MoD): the ministry "apologises that it fell short". The "failure was one of communication, not application", he said, adding the ministry was working hard to search documents across multiple IT systems and classifications at "huge expense".

QUOTE (Lord Justice Haddon-Cave, inquiry chair): the discovery was "troubling" and "extraordinary news"; he had taken the "exceptional step" of calling the hearing because of the disclosure and the "somewhat casual way" the MoD had informed his team; it was crucial that "any material of real relevance is quickly identified and disclosed".

QUOTE (Edward Craven KC, acting for the bereaved families): lawyers for the bereaved families said it was "staggering" the documents came to light at such a late stage in the inquiry's work; Craven said the disclosure represented "yet another example of the MoD frustrating the justice process" [BBC paraphrase — the words "yet another example of the MoD frustrating the justice process" are BBC's reported summary of Craven, NOT a verbatim quote].

QUOTE (Ministry of Defence): it was fully committed to supporting the inquiry and regretted that it was "not as prompt or consistent as it should have been" in disclosing the documents.
